subject: GIS grid values for habitat-specific abundance models

messages.author: 7595ad705c6bb0b8
messages.subject: GIS grid values for habitat-specific abundance models
parts:
Hello everyone,

I am trying an analysis to model abundance using the Sillett et al. (2012). Hierarchical distance sampling models to estimate population size and habitat-specific abundance of an island endemic study as a guide. 

My question for today is more about the GIS methods so please feel free to ignore or direct me to the adequate source. In this study to obtain the habitat-specific abundance values a grid of 2,787 9-ha cells was used. I am currently using a land-cover data set that has a specific resolution of 5 m and to obtain the values to the radius of my point count cut-off (30 m) I used a moving window analysis to get % per the class of interest. These values were used for my models.

However now I want to calculate at my landscape level using a 2-ha grid cell size, which should reduce the cell count total in the original raster. To obtain a value per 2-ha grid cell should I:

a) First re-sample my original raster to 2-ha resolution and then obtain the value from this output?
or
b) First obtain percentage land cover (moving window) at the 2-ha window size and then re-sample the raster output to 2-ha resolution? 

Now that I've written this, the option b seems redundant. Any thoughts, referrals would be greatly appreciated!

Kind Regards

messages.author: 403be63af7ebf220
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] GIS grid values for habitat-specific abundance models
parts:
Hi Fabiola,

Your questions raise many issues of scale that can't be easily addressed in a short email, but you might want to consider some of the ideas discussed in our recent paper: http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10980-016-0380-z. Unfortunately, it isn't possible to implement these methods in 'unmarked' yet, but you could try to implement them yourself.

Otherwise, a simpler approach would be to predict at the scale used in model fitting (5m resolution), and then aggregate your predictions up to the 2-ha scale. This should be fairly straight-forward.

Richard
